rewrites.summary:
Gibraltar legislates its own civil and criminal law as a self-governing territory on the Iberian peninsula's southern tip. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993 with an equal age of consent since 2012; discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment date from 2007; civil partnerships followed in 2014, and same-sex marriage was enacted unanimously in December 2016 after a 2015 public consultation returned overwhelming support (3,490 replies from a 24,117-person electorate).

For a transgender visitor the standing gap is legal gender: no route exists to change legal gender, and there was no specific hate-crime provision denigrating a person for sexual orientation until, in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice said it would 'urgently' consider one after a wave of online homophobia during Pride month drew a rare public rebuke from the head of government. Governance of the territory is subject to regular scrutiny by the UK parliament's overseas-territories committee, which has pressed accountability standards across the portfolio.

rewrites.summary:
Bermuda decriminalised private adult same-sex conduct in 1994 (House of Assembly, 22-16) and in 2013 outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriages performed in 2017 were withdrawn the following year by a Domestic Partnership Act — the first jurisdiction anywhere to reverse marriage equality — and in March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the traditional-marriage definition, so partnerships, not marriage, are the available status for same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the more telling fact is the protection gap: there is no legal recognition of transgender people, and therefore no gender-identity-specific discrimination protection at all. Church influence is significant in local politics — when a prominent entertainer's gay-charity cruise sought to dock in 2007 the premier's colourful defence was needed against religious objections — and the tourism economy that the island depends on has repeatedly had to be pointed at inclusivity.

There is no legal recognition of transgender people and thus no gender-identity discrimination protection. Church objections to LGBT visibility carry political weight, as in a 2007 dispute over a benefit cruise's docking rights that the government publicly rebuffed.

rewrites.summary:
Cayman law never held the criminalisation its earlier profile asserted: same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature refused, albeit with an unequal age of consent surviving the reform. In 2020 the Court of Appeal held that a same-sex couple's overseas marriage must be recognised, and in July 2021 roughly 600 people — including the premier, the governor and other ministers — joined the islands' first Pride parade, one of the broadest official turnouts a community there has seen.

The sharp turn came in 2022: a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect and, in March of that year, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rejected the challenge to it. Same-sex couples therefore have no marriage or civil-partnership status, the country that administers defence and foreign affairs declined to force the issue, and equality advocates have operated mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law itself.

In 2022 a statute confining family status to heterosexual marriage took effect, and in March that year the highest appellate committee in London rejected the challenge to it; same-sex couples consequently hold no marriage or partnership status, with protections advancing mainly through immigration and recognition rulings rather than family law.

rewrites.summary:
Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the administering state's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.

rewrites.summary:
Anguilla's prohibitions were removed around 2000-2001 — a recent first-person travel account puts the change at 2000, the contemporaneous wire coverage of the Caribbean-wide reform at January 2001 — again by imposition from London after local reluctance; the earlier profile's 'decriminalised 2019' appeared in no source and has been deleted. Same-sex relationships are simply not an issue in the public sense because there is almost no public LGBT life: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers and same-sex wedding tourism pitched on 'friendly, relaxed atmosphere.'

A queer family travelling openly in 2023 described the experience as uneventful on a 35-square-mile island. The practical visitor picture is quiet neutrality — nothing protects you much, and little opposes you at all.

rewrites.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures — the earlier claim of 'archaic criminal provisions on the books' was contradicted by the territory's own sources and has been removed. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.

A tiny, dispersed, private society in which neither hostility nor community is much visible.

rewrites.summary:
Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

The administering state's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.

rewrites.summary:
South Atlantic island settlement with its own assembly: same-sex activity legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005, and full equality in April 2017 when the assembly approved same-sex marriage and civil partnerships 7-1, on a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships — the registrar confirmed the law the following June, adoption followed the same year, the constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and the first Pride was held in the capital that April. An official of the community described it as 'open, tolerant and respectful'; note that the much more remote dependencies administered from the same capital did not follow on marriage.

The earlier profile's inherited arithmetic and its borrowed UK custody stories have been deleted: on the surviving evidence the legal picture here is stronger, not weaker, than the administering state's, and there is no source indicating the GB single-sex-services code extends to the territory.

Local officials describe an open, tolerant community; far more distant dependencies administered from the same capital did not follow suit on marriage. The administering state's equality-code machinery has no cited application here.

rewrites.summary:
A scattered South Atlantic territory of three island groups that legislated equality island by island: the 2009 constitutional order imposed by the administering state bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation across all three, and equal age of consent sits at 16. Marriage equality arrived in staggered fashion — the first dependency's council approved the ordinance 5-0 in May 2016 and it commenced January 2017, the most remote island followed in August 2017, and the principal island itself completed the set on 20 December 2017 — with adoption law following the same year.

The earlier profile undersold all of this as 'decriminalised' and added an unsourced 'church-conservative' gloss; neither survives the evidence. What is documented is a fast, orderly rights rollout across very small councils, and a total absence of survey data on social attitudes — remoteness, not resistance, is the characterised condition.

The prior profile's religion-and-conservatism gloss appeared in no source and was deleted; equally, no audited source surveys social attitudes in any of the three. rewrites.summary:
Pitcairn's roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves, and on paper they have adopted the most complete equality package in this group of territories: activity legal since 2001, a 2010 constitution that bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and a 2015 Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance — marriage defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity, foreign civil partnerships recognised, and adoption open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

The earlier profile's 'Christian-conservative, no public LGBT life' clause appeared in no source and has been deleted; it was the only stated basis for placing this territory below its administering state, which the legal record does not support. What the sources do say is that no islander is known to be in a same-sex relationship — on an island this size, invisibility is arithmetic rather than atmosphere, and defence is the administering state's responsibility.

rewrites.summary:
A self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, Guernsey moved briskly through the 2010s: in 2011 it aligned blood-donation rules with the metropole, ending the HIV-era ban on gay and bisexual donors; in June 2015 the states rewrote the adoption law to open adoption to same-sex couples, removing a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples; and in December 2015 the states approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting civil-partnership and secular-union alternatives as insufficient, with the law itself commencing from spring 2018.

That record covers sexual orientation squarely; the position on gender identity was asserted in the earlier profile without any cited source and has been deleted, so a transgender visitor should treat legal gender recognition and trans-specific protection as unestablished here — the more notable local quirk being that, on the documented chronology, civil partnership arrived later than in the neighbouring dependency that shares the island group's institutions.

rewrites.summary:
Isle of Man: a self-legislating Crown Dependency in the Irish Sea whose parliament, Tynwald, works through its own bills on these questions. The House of Keys in 2005 proactively adopted a clause protecting employees from dismissal over sexual orientation, framing it in human-rights terms; the chief minister publicly committed to marriage equality in 2015, at a time when this parliament and Northern Ireland's assembly were the only British legislatures refusing it; the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill passed its final legislative stages in April 2016 and the first civil partnership was converted to marriage that July, preserving the couple's 2015 wedding date.

Current reference material confirms the settled picture: civil partnerships from 2011, marriage since 2016, and a legal gender-recognition right in force since 2009 alongside 'gender reassignment' protections in island equality law. Claims about the metropole's single-sex code and its statutory guidance were carried in the earlier profile without primary legislative support and have been deleted, leaving the local record as the basis of this entry.
